newsitem.title: USA: U.S. condemns Hun Sen for Cambodia violence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. condemns Hun Sen for Cambodia violence.

text.p: The United States condemned Cambodian co-Prime Minister Hun Sen on Tuesday for using force to oust his rival Prince Norodom Ranariddh and said U.S. officials would meet the prince in Washington.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns expressed "strong opposition to the use of force to change the results of the 1993 election and the use of force by the forces of Hun Sen to effectively rupture the Paris accords of 1991."
Ranariddh was toppled at the weekend by Hun Sen, who had shared power with him in a fragile coalition government formed after United Nations-run elections in 1993.
Ranariddh, in Paris, told a news conference he was going to the United States on Wednesday to speak to the U.N. Security Council and later would meet top U.S. officials.
Burns confirmed U.S. officials would meet the prince, as an elected leader of his country, but was unable to say when. "I can tell you he will be received here at the State department," he said.

Burns said U.S. policy toward Cambodia would be based on four principles: The use of force is unacceptable and the principles of the 1991 Paris peace accords must be upheld; all parties, including Ranariddh's, must be allowed to operate freely; elections should go ahead as scheduled next year and no senior Khmer Rouge leaders should be allowed to play a role in Cambodian politics.
Hun Sen has accused Ranariddh of teaming up with Khmer Rouge deserters.

Ranariddh denied being in contact with the guerrilla group, reviled for its savage rule in the 1970s when more than one million Cambodians died, but said if they fought on his behalf in Cambodia, "there is nothing I can do about that."

Burns said the United States would consider over the next few days whether to continue with its aid programme to Cambodia. Washington allocated $35 million to Cambodia in the fiscal year ending in September.

In Paris, Ranariddh said Phnom Penh no longer qualified for international assistance as it no longer met the demands of donor nations and institutions which pledged $450 million in aid to Cambodia in Paris last week.
The donors had asked the government to ensure that the gains made since 1993 were not undermined by political instability.
Three U.S. warships, now in Japan, have been put on alert in case Washington orders an evacuation of its embassy and other personnel from Phnom Penh.
Pentagon spokeswoman Lt. Com. Karen Jeffries said the Dubuque left Sasebo on Tuesday, Washington time, and the other two ships in the amphibious group were to depart within hours.
They are headed for Okinawa, where they will pick up 2,022 U.S. Marines for exercises in that area, and could be in place to evacuate personnel from Cambodia within 4-1/2 days, she said.
Another U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, said it appeared the situation was easing in Cambodia after days of fighting between rival factions, making a U.S. evacuation less likely.
